1 1. Overview

This report explores the mathematical foundations of MCDM and Similarity Measures, focusing on their application in quantative decision-making and high-dimensional data analysis.

2 2. Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM)

2.1 2.1 AHP (Analytic Hierarchy Process)

AHP decomposes a problem into a Hierarchical Structure and uses pairwise comparisons to derive priorities.

  • Step 1: Construct Pairwise Comparison Matrix (\(A\)) For \(n\) criteria, construct a matrix where \(a_{ij}\) represents the relative importance of element \(i\) over element \(j\). \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & a_{12} & \cdots & a_{1n} \\ 1/a_{12} & 1 & \cdots & a_{2n} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1/a_{1n} & 1/a_{2n} & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] (Property: \(a_{ji} = 1/a_{ij}, \quad a_{ii} = 1\))

  • Step 2: Calculate Priority Vector (\(w\)) Mathematically, this involves solving the eigenvalue problem: \[A \cdot w = \lambda_{max} \cdot w\] In practice (Synthesization method):

    1. Normalize each column of \(A\): \(\bar{a}_{ij} = \frac{a_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_{kj}}\)
    2. Average the rows to find weights: \(w_i = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{n} \bar{a}_{ij}}{n}\)

  • Step 3: Consistency Verification To ensure the decision maker’s logic is consistent:

    1. Calculate Consistency Index (CI): \(CI = \frac{\lambda_{max} - n}{n - 1}\)
    2. Calculate Consistency Ratio (CR): \(CR = \frac{CI}{RI}\) (Where \(RI\) is the Random Index based on matrix size \(n\). If \(CR < 0.1\), consistency is acceptable.)
TipInsight: Handling Subjectivity

The core strength of AHP lies in the Consistency Ratio (CR). Unlike simple weighted scoring, AHP mathematically quantifies ‘how inconsistent the decision maker is.’ If \(CR > 0.1\), it forces the decision maker to re-evaluate their logic, ensuring rational consistency in subjective judgments.

2.2 2.2 ANP (Analytic Network Process)

ANP generalizes AHP by overcoming the assumption of independence among criteria, handling interdependence using a supermatrix approach.

  • Step 1: Construct Unweighted Supermatrix Perform pairwise comparisons (like AHP) for all interacting clusters and nodes. Place the resulting local priority vectors into a block matrix. \[W_{unweighted} = \begin{bmatrix} W_{11} & W_{12} \\ W_{21} & W_{22} \end{bmatrix}\]

  • Step 2: Construct Weighted Supermatrix Since the unweighted matrix is not column-stochastic (columns sum > 1), multiply each block by the priority of its corresponding cluster so that each column sums to 1. \[W_{weighted} = W_{unweighted} \times W_{cluster}\]

  • Step 3: Calculate Limiting Supermatrix Raise the weighted supermatrix to a large power \(k\) to capture all indirect influences until the values stabilize (converge). \[\lim_{k \to \infty} W^k\] The resulting rows represent the final global priorities of the elements.

NoteWhy ANP matters in Engineering?

Real-world industrial systems are rarely linear hierarchies. For instance, Product Quality affects Sales, but increased Sales might lower Quality due to production pressure (Feedback Loop). ANP captures this interdependence via the Supermatrix, making it superior for complex system modeling.

2.3 2.3 DEMATEL

DEMATEL is specialized for visualizing the Cause & Effect structure of complex factors.

  • Step 1: Direct Relation Matrix (\(A\)) Create an \(n \times n\) matrix based on expert evaluation (scale 0~4), where \(a_{ij}\) is the direct influence of \(i\) on \(j\).

  • Step 2: Normalization (\(X\)) Normalize the matrix so that values fall between 0 and 1. \[k = \frac{1}{\max_{1 \le i \le n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} a_{ij}}\] \[X = k \cdot A\]

  • Step 3: Total Relation Matrix (\(T\)) Calculate the sum of direct and all indirect effects using the geometric series formula (where \(I\) is the identity matrix): \[T = X + X^2 + X^3 + \dots = X(I - X)^{-1}\]

  • Step 4: Causal Parameters

    • Prominence (\(D+R\)): \(D_i\) (Row sum) + \(R_i\) (Col sum). Represents total importance.
    • Relation (\(D-R\)): If positive, factor \(i\) is a Cause; if negative, it is an Effect.

2.4 2.4 TOPSIS

TOPSIS ranks alternatives based on their geometric distance to ideal solutions.

NoteKey Concept
  • PIS (Positive Ideal Solution, \(A^*\)): The hypothetical solution that maximizes benefit and minimizes cost.
  • NIS (Negative Ideal Solution, \(A^-\)): The hypothetical solution that minimizes benefit and maximizes cost.

  • Step 1: Vector Normalization Normalize the decision matrix (\(x_{ij}\)) to eliminate unit differences. \[r_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{m} x_{kj}^2}}\]

  • Step 2: Weighted Normalized Matrix (\(v\)) Multiply by the weights (\(w_j\)) of each criterion. \[v_{ij} = w_j \cdot r_{ij}\]

  • Step 3: Determine Ideal Solutions

    • PIS (\(A^*\)): Max value for benefits (\(J+\)), Min value for costs (\(J-\)). \[A^* = \{ (\max_i v_{ij} | j \in J+), (\min_i v_{ij} | j \in J-) \}\]
    • NIS (\(A^-\)): Min value for benefits (\(J+\)), Max value for costs (\(J-\)). \[A^- = \{ (\min_i v_{ij} | j \in J+), (\max_i v_{ij} | j \in J-) \}\]

  • Step 4: Calculate Distances & Closeness

    • Separation from PIS: \(S_i^* = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n} (v_{ij} - v_j^*)^2}\)
    • Separation from NIS: \(S_i^- = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{n} (v_{ij} - v_j^-)^2}\)
    • Relative Closeness (\(C_i^*\)): \[C_i^* = \frac{S_i^-}{S_i^* + S_i^-}\] (Rank alternatives by \(C_i^*\) in descending order.)

3 3. Measurement Metrics

These measures provide the mathematical foundation for quantifying relationships between data objects.

3.1 3.1 Similarity Measures

  • Cosine Similarity: Measures the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors. It focuses on orientation rather than magnitude. \[\text{similarity}(A, B) = \frac{A \cdot B}{\|A\| \|B\|} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i B_i}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i^2} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} B_i^2}}\] (Range: 0 to 1 for positive vector spaces)

  • Jaccard Index: Measures similarity between finite sample sets. \[J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|}\]

3.2 3.2 Distance Measures

  • Euclidean Distance: The straight-line distance between two points in Euclidean space (\(L_2\) norm). \[D(A, B) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (A_i - B_i)^2}\]

  • Manhattan Distance: The distance between two points measured along axes at right angles (\(L_1\) norm). \[MD(P, Q) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} |p_i - q_i|\]

  • Hellinger Distance: Used to quantify the similarity between two probability distributions. \[H(P, Q) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (\sqrt{p_i} - \sqrt{q_i})^2}\]

WarningThe Curse of Dimensionality

In high-dimensional spaces (e.g., text data with 10,000+ features), the relative difference between the nearest and farthest data points becomes negligible. Thus, Euclidean Distance often loses its discriminatory power. In such sparse environments, Cosine Similarity is generally preferred as it focuses on the “direction” rather than the magnitude.

3.3 3.3 Node Centrality (Network Analysis)

Measures the importance of nodes within a graph.

Measure Definition
Degree Centrality The number of direct links connected to a node.
Closeness Centrality The reciprocal of the sum of the shortest path distances from a node to all other nodes.
\(C_c(x) = \frac{1}{\sum_y d(y, x)}\)
Betweenness Centrality The extent to which a node lies on the shortest paths between other nodes.
Eigenvector Centrality A measure of influence where connections to high-scoring nodes contribute more to the score.
